title: May minutes trace the third Australian hike to fuel pass-through and domestic capacity
summary: The 4–5 May meeting ended in an 8–1 vote to lift the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.35%. The minutes appeared on 19 May. This was the third consecutive increase. The majority’s concern was the persistence of underlying inflation in an economy already close to capacity before energy supplies were disrupted. One member thought the original excess demand smaller and the eventual damage to spending from a prolonged conflict larger. The disagreement is significant for forecasting. Both sides could see the same surge in the current price of petrol, yet reach a different rate decision because they expected different outcomes for employment, demand and price-setting over the next two years (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

March headline inflation stood at 4.6% from a year earlier. Higher fuel prices contributed 0.8 percentage points. The temporary fuel-excise reduction beginning 1 April was estimated to subtract about 0.5 percentage points from annual inflation in April. Both quantities concern the published price index and have different reference months. Neither measures how far firms would later pass higher freight costs into food, goods or services. Liaison indicated that many consumer-facing businesses had still to pass on the increase, yet a growing proportion expected larger than usual price increases over the coming year. Staff analysis suggested pass-through tends to be faster and more complete when inflation is already elevated. Longer-term inflation beliefs remained consistent with target even as short-term measures rose (Economic conditions).

The supply disruption was sizeable. Staff estimated reductions of roughly 10% in global oil supply and 20% in liquefied natural gas supply. Oil prices in real terms remained below peaks in several preceding episodes. Global oil intensity was about half its early-1990s level, and demand for components used in AI investment continued to support several East Asian trading partners. Higher LNG and thermal coal prices could support Australia’s aggregate income while higher petrol bills reduced household purchasing power. Domestic spending data offered little sign yet of a broad collapse. Card spending at petrol stations rose without an obvious offset elsewhere. The sample was early and the shock unevenly distributed, making it premature to infer that consumers would absorb the entire increase indefinitely (Financial conditions and Economic conditions).

The global financial response was uneven across assets. Equities had recovered from an initial decline as earnings forecasts improved in some industries, including semiconductors. Corporate spreads returned to historically low levels even though surveys of consumers and businesses showed sharp falls in confidence. Policy-rate paths for end-2026 had risen roughly 50–60 basis points in several advanced economies. Much of the rise in longer government yields reflected real yields, with longer-term inflation compensation relatively stable. For Australia, a widening yield differential and commodity prices supported the trade-weighted currency. The Board considered both the possibility that markets underestimated adverse outcomes and the possibility that the resilience of output and profits had genuine economic foundations (Financial conditions).

By May, banks had largely passed the February and March increases into advertised rates. Cash payments by existing mortgage borrowers adjust with a lag because lenders must give notice and repayment dates differ. The established housing market was already softer, while business and household credit volumes had yet to slow substantially and funding remained readily available. Market prices implied around a 75% chance of a quarter-point increase at this meeting and a total rise of about 60 basis points from the prevailing cash rate by year-end. Model estimates placed the rate near the upper part of the range of neutral estimates, with considerable uncertainty about inflation expectations and structural investment demand. Members therefore declined to treat a model threshold or an unchanged credit growth rate as decisive (Financial conditions).

Staff’s baseline used 29 April market prices. It assumed a further 60 basis points of rate increases during 2026 and gradually lower oil prices as the conflict resolved. GDP growth would trough at 1.3% in six to twelve months, still positive but below potential. Unemployment would reach 4.7% by mid-2028. Headline inflation would peak at 4.8% in the June quarter and move back into target range around mid-2027. Trimmed mean inflation would still exceed 3% at that point and reach 2.5% only in mid-2028. The baseline thus combined a decline in fuel’s direct contribution with a slower unwinding of domestic inflationary pressure. The projected return to target had additional tightening built into it (Economic outlook).

The two adverse scenarios produce different medium-term inflation signs. In both, a longer conflict creates a stronger initial surge in energy costs. In the first, underlying inflation remains above baseline throughout the forecast. In the second, confidence falls sufficiently to depress global and domestic spending further, opening more spare capacity. By 2028 underlying inflation in that scenario is below baseline. Neither scenario included a permanent loss of productive capacity. Such a loss would change how much output could recover without renewed inflation. The distinction explains why evidence about households’ decision to use their savings matters as much as the latest barrel price once the forecast extends beyond the initial shock (Economic outlook).

Eight members saw an inflation forecast remaining too high for too long and were willing to accept some easing in a still-tight labour market to improve that outlook. The dissenter saw more value in observing the lagged effects of the 50 basis points already delivered. That member also saw little current evidence of an unanchoring of longer-run expectations. Members judged overall conditions would probably be somewhat restrictive after the decision, giving them time to assess subsequent effects. In a separate discussion, they reviewed principles, decision procedures and governance for additional monetary tools should rates again approach very low levels. Governance Board feedback was to precede formal approval. That preparatory work created no new operation at the May meeting (Considerations for monetary policy and Framework for additional monetary policy tools).

Comparisons with foreign central banks supported different positions within the Board. Several peers had waited for clarity on energy, an example cited by the dissenter. Yet some of those economies were starting with negative output gaps, while Australia was assessed to have excess demand. A shared supply shock could therefore warrant different timing even under similar mandates. Matching countries only on their realised headline inflation would miss this starting condition (Financial conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

questions.question: Was the broadening of firms’ pricing intentions followed by actual selling-price increases?
questions.detail: Match liaison or firm-survey responses to subsequent prices, quantities and operating margins. Compare fuel-intensive products with low-exposure products under similar demand conditions. Control for the excise change and its reversal. Greater intentions may represent a plan contingent on competitors also raising prices, so an intentions index alone cannot establish the size or duration of pass-through.

questions.question: Could a confidence collapse push underlying inflation below baseline despite more expensive energy?
questions.detail: Observe realised spending, hours and investment alongside consumer and business sentiment, paying attention to households’ liquid buffers. Compare regions and industries with different energy exposure and export incomes. A fall in confidence that does not precede changes in expenditure gives limited support to the second adverse scenario. If supply capacity also falls persistently, re-estimate the output gap rather than assuming the same disinflationary response.

questions.question: How much tightening had reached existing borrowers by the May meeting?
questions.detail: Track new advertised rates, notification dates, required mortgage instalments and actual cash transfers separately for the February, March and May moves. Compare discretionary purchases of households paid on similar schedules but facing different mortgage reset dates. Keep pre-meeting market pricing distinct from post-release returns. The magnitude of the final vote does not reveal how much of the policy path had already reached private cash flows.
